title: Request-Response Patterns
description: Explore common request-response patterns for synchronous microservices communication.

data.text: Request-response is the most common communication pattern in microservices, but it comes with challenges like timeout handling, retries, and circuit breaking. Google and Netflix have published extensive guidelines on implementing robust request-response patterns.

data.title: Patterns Overview
items: Direct call: Caller directly invokes callee (simple but fragile)
API composition: API Gateway or aggregator combines multiple service calls
Backend for Frontend (BFF): Custom API per client type
GraphQL: Single endpoint with flexible queries

data.text: In the API composition pattern, a single service (often an API Gateway or a dedicated composition service) aggregates data from multiple downstream services. This reduces the number of round-trips for clients but introduces coupling to the aggregator.

data.title: N+1 Problem
data.text: API composition can cause the N+1 problem: fetching N items requires N+1 queries. Use batching or GraphQL to reduce round-trips.

data.title: Example: API Composition for Product Page
data.code: A product page needs data from Product, Inventory, and Pricing services. An API Gateway composes these into a single response.

# Without composition: Client makes 3 calls
GET /products/123
GET /products/123/inventory
GET /products/123/pricing

# With composition: Client makes 1 call
GET /products/123?include=inventory,pricing
# Gateway internally calls:
# - Product Service
# - Inventory Service
# - Pricing Service
# And returns combined response

data.caption: API composition pattern
data.definition:
graph LR
    C[Client] --> G[API Gateway]
    G --> P[Product Service]
    G --> I[Inventory Service]
    G --> PR[Pricing Service]
    P --> G
    I --> G
    PR --> G
    G --> C

items.question: What is the difference between API Gateway and BFF?
items.answer: API Gateway is a generic entry point for all clients. BFF is a custom API built specifically for one client type (e.g., mobile, web). BFFs often sit behind the API Gateway.

items.question: How do I handle timeouts?
items.answer: Set reasonable timeouts on all outbound calls. Use circuit breakers to fail fast when a service is down. Netflix Hystrix and Polly are popular libraries for this.

items.question: Should I retry failed requests?
items.answer: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter for transient failures. Never retry non-idempotent operations (like payment charges) without careful consideration.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Request-response is simple but requires careful timeout and retry handling
BFFs provide tailored APIs for specific clients
Always handle failures gracefully in request-response chains
data.takeaway: Design request-response patterns with failure in mind; assume every external call can fail.
